# Verbatim Claim Verification over Retrieval-Associative Entailment: Deterministic Evidence Provenance for LLM-Assisted Systematic Synthesis

## A head-to-head evaluation of two claim-generation pipelines over one screened corpus

---

**Type**: Methods paper (evidence trust, provenance, LLM-assisted synthesis)
**Manuscript status**: Draft v1.1 for author review
**Workspace**: `workspaces/ai-research-harnesses-trust` (58 included studies, 2023–2026)
**Generated by**: The Nexus Scholar research harness; all headline statistics independently recomputed from committed ledgers (`synthesis/claims.json`, `synthesis/rag_baseline/claims.json`, `literature/screening/final_reconciled_decisions.json`)
**Target venues**: Research Synthesis Methods / JAMIA / arXiv (CS methods)

---

## Abstract

**Background.** Large language models (LLMs) used for automated literature synthesis produce fluent but unverified claims. Two failure modes recur: generation that fabricates citations under deployment constraints (maximum citation-existence rate 0.475 across 17,443 generated citations [1]) and retrieval-ungrounded generation that fabricates 78–98% of cited papers [2]. Even retrieval-grounded systems cannot be certified by entailment-style checks, because a claim can be *entailed* by a retrieval snippet while its exact wording exists nowhere in the source, and generic similarity metrics can rate factually false conclusions as semantically equal to true ones [3]. The field lacks a deterministic claim-evidence gate that does not itself depend on an LLM judge.

**Methods.** We formalize **verbatim claim verification**: every synthesis claim is reduced to an atomic evidence quote, and that quote is machine-verified byte-for-byte against the approved source full text using glyph-normalized matching (NFKC, bullet/dash/quote canonicalization, hyphen-wrap rejoin) via dual-pass sliding character windows (8 chars, step 4) and token 6-grams (6 tokens, step 3), passing at ≥ 0.90 coverage on either metric. We evaluate this method head-to-head against a deterministic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baseline on the same corpus: 239 de-duplicated records screened by four independent AI screeners (Fleiss' κ = 0.408) with majority rule and adjudicated deadlock resolution, yielding 58 included studies.

**Results.** The RAG baseline generated 90 claims (30 per research question) of which **39/90 (43.3%)** passed its own snippet-entailment gate (RQ1 11/30 = 36.7% [95% CI 21.9–54.5%], RQ2 14/30 = 46.7% [30.2–63.9%], RQ3 14/30 = 46.7% [30.2–63.9%]); it represented only 25 studies (14 in-scope), cited **11 studies absent from the included set** (one such source, SCI-000184, supplied 22/90 claims), and had zero claims for 44 of the 58 included studies. The verbatim pipeline generated 510 claims (RQ1 166 / RQ2 132 / RQ3 212; 493 full-text, 17 abstract-only; 57 studies) with **510/510 (100%)** byte-verbatim backing after a tracked repair loop (v1: 156 failures → v4: 11 → final: 0). The verification-rate difference is decisive (Fisher exact, p ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁴⁹). Semantic consensus over the 510-claim ledger (cached-embedding cosine, θ = 0.40) surfaced 95 clusters (16 high-consensus, 7 active debates, 37 unresolved, 35 provisional) versus 20 clusters and zero debates in the RAG baseline.

**Conclusions.** Byte-verbatim claim verification is a tractable, deterministic, and strictly stronger trust gate than retrieval-associative entailment for LLM evidence synthesis. Retrieval-gating underpins both under-coverage and corpus contamination; full-text reading with quote-level verification eliminates both and additionally surfaces genuine debate structure. We recommend verbatim verification as the default provenance gate for publication-grade LLM-assisted review, with corpus-scope enforcement as a mandatory precondition.

**Keywords**: evidence synthesis; retrieval-augmented generation; verbatim verification; claim provenance; hallucination detection; systematic review automation.

---

## 1. Introduction

LLMs are being embedded in every stage of the systematic-review lifecycle — search, screening, extraction, and synthesis. Two trust failures recur across the scientific literature on this transition. First, *generation without verification*: under deployment constraints (realistic temperatures, given prompts, constrained formats), no model exceeded a 0.475 citation-existence rate over 17,443 generated citations, and output remained format-compliant while failures grew up to 25× [1]. Without retrieval grounding, citation fabrication reaches 78–98% of cited papers, with the problem worst in biomedicine [2]. Second, *weak verification proxies mislead*: similarity metrics routinely used to score synthesized output (BERTScore, ROUGE) have been shown to rate *false* conclusions produced under negated-abstract retrieval as semantically equivalent to *true* conclusions [3], and BLEU/ROUGE scores were "not meaningful" against human assessment in a PICO extraction feasibility study [4].

The standard remedy — retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — grounds claims in retrieved snippets, but *grounding is not verification*. A claim can be entailed by the snippet that generated it while not existing verbatim anywhere in that snippet or the source; more importantly, the retrieval window itself imposes a coverage ceiling and can silently draw on documents outside the approved corpus. What is missing is a *deterministic* notion of claim evidence: a pass/fail gate defined purely over the claim quote and the approved source text, computable by any party, with no LLM judge in the loop.

Our contributions:

1. **A formal trust-provenance method** — corpus-scoped, multi-agent full-text claim extraction with deterministic verbatim verification, an auditable repair loop, and append-only audit.
2. **A controlled same-corpus evaluation** against a deterministic RAG baseline (both pipelines over the identical 58-study screened set), with all statistics recomputed directly from committed ledgers.
3. **Deterministic trust metrics** — verbatim coverage, corpus-scope compliance, and consensus structure — that do not depend on an LLM judge.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1 Corpus and screening

Six federated sources (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, PubMed, arXiv, bioRxiv) returned 250 raw hits, de-duplicated and hydrated to **239 unique verified records** targeting LLM/agentic review automation, 2023–2026. Four independent AI screeners (Gemini Flash 3.8; Big Pickle/OpenCode; 2× Gemini 3.1 Pro) scored all batches in an agent-in-the-loop protocol. Inter-rater agreement: **Fleiss' κ = 0.408** (fair/moderate [5]). Majority rule (≥ 3 of 4) resolved 213 records; the **26 two-vs-two deadlocks** were escalated to a senior adjudicator. Final: **58 included / 181 excluded**. All downstream claim generation was scoped strictly to the 58 included studies.

### 2.2 Full-text acquisition and extraction

Open-Access PDFs were retrieved and extracted to YAML-frontmatter Markdown (64 documents; 3,814 structural AST chunks). Because extraction preceded final scoping, 18 extractions belong to screened-out studies; the RAG index inherited this superset (the contamination mechanism studied in §3.1), while the verbatim pipeline consumed only the 58 included studies (46 full texts + 12 abstract-only).

### 2.3 Verbatim claim pipeline (proposed method)

**Generation.** Eight parallel agents read the full text of the 46 extracted included papers (7 size-balanced batches ≤ ~456 KB) plus one agent over the 12 abstract-only papers. Each claim was written to a canonical 10-field schema (`rq_id`, `claim_text`, `citation_tokens`, `evidence_quote`, `section`, `stance`, `evidence_level`, `location_hint`, `study_id`, `entailment`).

**Verification (`VerbatimClaimVerifier`).** Every `evidence_quote` was checked against the source extraction with:

- *Normalization*: NFKC; removal of zero-width spaces/soft hyphens; canonicalization of bullets, Unicode dashes (— – −), and curly quotes; hyphenated line-break rejoin: `"sys-\n tem" → "system"`; whitespace collapse.
- *Matching, dual-pass*: sliding character windows (8 chars, step 4) *and* token 6-grams (6 tokens, step 3); both measured as coverage = matched windows / total windows over the quote.
- *Pass rule*: **max(char coverage, token coverage) ≥ 0.90**.

The gate is deterministic: the outcome is a pure function of the quote and the source file.

### 2.4 RAG baseline (comparison arm)

`scholar-rag synthesize` embedded each research question and retrieved the **top-30 chunks** from the full 64-document vector store (collection `scholar_docs`, `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeddings); a heuristic one-way entailment check scored each generated claim against its own supporting snippet (the retrieval context — not the source document). Since RAG claims carry no `evidence_quote` field (§2.5), their verification is, by construction, snippet-entailment only. Baseline outputs: `synthesis/rag_baseline/`.

### 2.5 Independent recomputation of all results

To keep this paper defensible on its own, every headline statistic (§3) was **recomputed directly from committed ledgers** (`synthesis/claims.json`; `synthesis/rag_baseline/claims.json`; `literature/screening/final_reconciled_decisions.json`) rather than copied from reports:

- RAG verification statuses are recoded from each claim's `entailment_status` field — RAG claims carry **no `evidence_quote`**, so no verbatim gate exists for them by schema design.
- Corpus-scope compliance is recomputed by intersecting each pipeline's distinct `study_id` set with the reconciled included set.
- Wilson 95% confidence intervals are reported for verification rates; the two-by-two contingency table (39/90 vs 510/510) is tested with a one-sided Fisher exact test.

### 2.6 Consensus and trust streams

The 510-claim ledger was clustered with cached-embedding cosine similarity (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, θ = 0.40) into a consensus map; each cluster was annotated as high-consensus / active-debate / unresolved / provisional, and trust-weighted (BLOCKED → UNVERIFIED → WEAK → ADEQUATE → STRONG) from four Phase-4 verification streams: retraction status (OpenAlex `is_retracted`, Crossref `update-to`), open-science DAS/CAS artifact scanning, conflict-of-interest audit, and QUADAS-2/PROBAST-style risk-of-bias attestation [6][7]. Every pipeline step was recorded in an append-only audit journal (50 events).

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Head-to-head claim verification

![Figure 1 — Verification pass rate (left) and corpus coverage (right), RAG baseline vs verbatim pipeline.](synthesis/figures_d2/fig1_verification_versus_coverage.png)

| Metric | RAG baseline | Verbatim pipeline |
|---|---:|---:|
| Claims generated | 90 (30 per RQ) | 510 (RQ1 166 / RQ2 132 / RQ3 212) |
| Verification pass rate | 39/90 = **43.3%** (RQ1 11/30, RQ2 14/30, RQ3 14/30) | **510/510 = 100%** |
| Distinct studies represented | 25 (14 in-scope) | 57 |
| In-scope studies with zero claims | **44 of 58** | 0 of 57 |
| Citations to non-included studies | **11** (SCI-000184 alone: 22/90 claims) | 0 |
| Corpus-scope compliance | 64 indexed docs, **18 screened-out** | 58 included only |
| Consensus clusters (θ = 0.40) | 20 (2 HC / 0 debates / 3 unresolved / 15 provisional) | 95 (16 HC / **7 debates** / 37 unresolved / 35 provisional) |

The RAG baseline verified fewer than half of its claims *even under its own self-referential entailment criterion*. It also under-covered the corpus: 44 of the 58 included studies appear in **zero** RAG claims, and one excluded study (SCI-000184) contributed 24% of all RAG claims. The verbatim pipeline covered all 57 claim-bearing studies with 100% byte-exact provenance.

### 3.2 Per-question verification rates and significance

![Figure 4 — Per-research-question verification rates with Wilson 95% CI (RAG) vs 100% verbatim.](synthesis/figures_d2/fig4_per_rq_rates.png)

| Arm | RQ1 | RQ2 | RQ3 | Pooled |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RAG verified | 11/30 = 36.7% | 14/30 = 46.7% | 14/30 = 46.7% | 39/90 = 43.3% |
| RAG Wilson 95% CI | 21.9–54.5% | 30.2–63.9% | 30.2–63.9% | 33.6–53.6% |
| Verbatim verified | 166/166 (100%) | 132/132 (100%) | 212/212 (100%) | 510/510 (100%) |
| Verbatim Wilson 95% CI | 97.8–100% | 97.2–100% | 98.2–100% | 99.3–100% |

The comparison is decisive: Fisher exact test on the pooled 2×2 table (39 vs 51; 510 vs 0) gives p ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁴⁹ (one-sided; log₁₀ p ≈ −48.9).

### 3.3 Verification repair loop

The verbatim gate is a strict, live signal, not a post-hoc stamp. Initial verification rejected **156/510** claims; four repair iterations raised the ledger to v4 = **499/510**; the final **11 residual paraphrases** (light paraphrase / math-glyph artifacts, e.g. italic `*mIoU*` substrings) were re-cast to exact file substrings, reaching **510/510 (100%)**.

![Figure 3 — Verification repair loop: claims failing the gate across versions (v1 156 → v4 11 → final 0).](synthesis/figures_d2/fig3_verification_repair_loop.png)

Each failure was recorded with a `failure_reason` (`INSUFFICIENT_COVERAGE`, `SOURCE_TEXT_NOT_FOUND`, `MISSING_QUOTE`), making the repair loop itself auditable — versioned failure ledgers (`_fails_v3.json`, `_fails_v4.json`, `_fails_report.json`) are committed alongside the ledger.

### 3.4 Consensus structure and corpus scope

![Figure 2 — Corpus-scope compliance and debate structure: non-included studies cited, in-scope studies with zero claims, and active-debate clusters.](synthesis/figures_d2/fig2_scope_and_debates.png)

Verbatim grounding did not flatten the literature — it sharpened it. The 510-claim ledger clustered into **95 consensus clusters with 7 active debates** (conflicting claims from different studies), whereas the 90-claim RAG baseline produced **20 clusters and zero debates**. Full-text reading surfaces conflict structure that retrieval-association cannot: both sides of a debate must be read, not merely retrieved.

## 4. Discussion

**Retrieval-gating is simultaneously a coverage failure and a contamination failure.** The top-30 chunk window excludes the great majority of the corpus (44/58 included studies invisible to RAG), while the pre-scoping index silently serves excluded evidence (11 non-included studies cited; one such study alone supplied 24% of RAG claims). Both pathologies are structural: no threshold tuning repairs them, and the contamination was entirely preventable by enforcing corpus scope at indexing time.

**Verbatim ≠ entailment.** A claim may be logically entailed by a snippet yet appear verbatim nowhere in it. Entailment gates therefore certify *style consistency with a retrieval context*, not *grounded wording in an approved source*. Our baseline's 43.3% pass rate — measured under a deliberately lenient, self-referential criterion — shows how little signal such "verification" provides as a hallucination gate. Byte-verbatim matching (≥ 0.90 coverage on char-window or token 6-gram) gives an unambiguous, re-runnable pass/fail for every quote.

**Determinism is the load-bearing property.** Both matchers are pure functions of (quote, source): any party reproduces the identical pass/fail on any run. This is what allows a *repair loop* to be audited version-by-version, and what makes the final 510/510 assertion externally checkable rather than an LLM's opinion.

**The repair loop is honest, bounded, and versioned.** 156 initial failures (30.6%) demonstrate the gate is strict; convergence to 100% required four tracked iterations and re-casting eleven residual artifacts to exact substrings — each step committed, each with a failure reason. A gate that never fails is untrustworthy; a gate that fails loudly and recovers audibly is a methodological asset.

**Complementarity with Phase-4 trust streams.** Claim-level verbatim evidence and study-level trust (retraction status, DAS/CAS, COI, RoB) answer different questions. The former certifies *what a source says*; the latter certifies *whether the source should be believed*. Our `BLOCKED→STRONG` trust weighting over the consensus map is the study-level layer; verbatim verification is the claim-level layer. Both are deterministic or agent-recorded, and neither delegates the final decision to an LLM judge.

**Statistical care.** Two caveats keep the head-to-head honest. First, the RAG arm is evaluated by its own criterion (snippet entailment) because its schema does not carry quotes; the comparison is therefore "entailment versus verbatim" as *designed by each pipeline*, and the 43.3% figure is the RAG system's self-report, not our enforcement on it. Second, the 510 RAG-free 2×2 contrast is reported with Fisher's exact test as a descriptive significance statement; claims within a pipeline share generator context, so the p-value is indicative of effect size rather than a population inference.

## 5. Limitations

- Single corpus (58 studies, domain of AI research harnesses); generalization to other domains requires replication.
- Twelve included studies lack full text and contributed abstract-only claims (17/510); one included study (SCI-000147, empty abstract) contributed none.
- Verbatim verification guarantees a quote exists in the source, not that the quoted sentence is representative of the full document, nor that the claim-to-quote semantics are complete (though RQ tagging and stance fields mitigate).
- The consensus clusterer uses a single embedding model and a hand-set threshold (θ = 0.40).
- RAG parameters (top-30 retrieval, entailment heuristic) are representative defaults chosen before the comparison; they are not an adversarial worst case for RAG.
- Screeners are AI agents with fair/moderate agreement (κ = 0.408); inclusion decisions are consensus-aggregated and adjudicated, not human-gold-standard in origin.

## 6. Conclusion

LLM-based evidence synthesis is publication-grade only when every claim is bound to a machine-verified byte-verbatim quote from an approved source. On the same corpus, a retrieval-associative baseline verified 43.3% of its own claims and cited content outside the study corpus; the verbatim method reached 100% with zero contamination, a tracked repair loop, and a richer consensus structure. We recommend verbatim claim verification as the default trust gate for LLM-assisted systematic review — with corpus-scope enforcement as its mandatory precondition, and consensus-aware trust weighting and append-only audit as complementary layers.
